Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers: Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search, all deeply integrated.

Sources indicate that developers decide what to build with by listening to people they trust, much of it on Twitter, where Supabase's community, debuts, and competitors are all discussed in public. We want a senior DevRel leader who is already a known, trusted voice there, to be a brand ambassador for Supabase. You'll work alongside our Latest Media and DevRel teams and help shape how Supabase shows up in these conversations. We hire for the voice and following you already have.

Be a visible, trusted voice for Supabase on Twitter: post, reply, and join developer conversations daily.

Share sharp, useful content, from launches and tips to opinions on where building is going.

Represent Supabase at events, on podcasts, and in the wider developer community.

Bring developer feedback to engineering and product, and work with Upcoming Media, DevRel, and PMM on launches.

Industry observers note that you have an existing, engaged Twitter following. We'll look at who you talk to and how people respond, as well as follower count.

You have senior experience in DevRel, developer advocacy, or a similar developer-facing role.

You're credible with a technical audience and a strong writer with a distinctive voice.

You're comfortable representing a manufacturer publicly, on camera, on stage, and online.

In a recent development, we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Recent findings suggest that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

In a recent development, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire tech giant gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

In a recent development, we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
  • Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to .
  • Grokipedia reveals that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

Nearly there — check your email.

Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Grokipedia reveals that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

According to recent reports, when I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia said “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”.

I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

Recent findings suggest that that article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which released a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D. (Editor’s note: After this article was published, someone updated the inaccurate Grok pages. The original versions are linked here.).

Still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds latest content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it demonstrates how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

In a recent development, musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he stated was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a newly introduced version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had big aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia highlights edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors revealed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too rapidly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites.

It has been revealed that wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.).

By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder.

Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times.

In a recent development, despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models.

In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race.

Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok mentioned I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor.

The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes indicated Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a significant scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article stated had an impact on “late-election discourse.”.

I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop.

Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s key and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important.

In a recent development, the writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.”.

Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter.

Industry observers note that bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My substantial takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok demonstrates that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

Recent findings suggest that winona is one of the leading telemedicine companies providing HRT for women in menopause. At Winona, copy isn’t just about sounding nice. It’s a measurable variable in our growth funnel. You will design and execute rapid copy experiments across our paid acquisition, intake flows, and lifecycle retention loops to help women confidently access bioidentical HRT and menopause care.

Full-Funnel Experimentation. Write copy hypotheses, design rapid A/B tests alongside growth and analytics teams, analyze performance data, and turn winning variations into a scalable messaging playbook.

High-Intent Conversion Surfaces. Own the persuasive strategy and microcopy for landing pages, interactive quiz/intake flows, checkouts, and dynamic pricing/offer messaging.

Industry observers note that paid Acquisition at Scale. Generate volume-driven concepts, hooks, and static/video copy variants for Meta, Google, and YouTube, systematically iterating based on creative testing data.

In a recent development, voice of Customer (VoC) Intelligence. Continuously mine product reviews, customer support tickets, intake data, and exit surveys to isolate deep qualitative insights and high-converting customer language.

AI-Augmented Workflows. Leverage and train Winona’s internal AI copywriting tools to scale production velocity, maintain brand consistency, and build automated variant pipelines without sacrificing quality.

5+ years of dedicated copywriting experience specializing in direct-response, conversion copywriting, or growth marketing.

According to recent reports, DTC Telehealth, Wellness, or HealthTech experience is highly preferred. You understand how to write about sensitive health topics with clinical authority and deep empathy.

A portfolio backed by data and results — the exact copy variants you tested, the structural or psychological changes you made, and the quantifiable lift they produced in metrics like CTR, quiz completion, or conversion rates.

In a recent development, deep lifecycle marketing mastery: significant experience building and optimizing automated email and SMS flows (onboarding, retention, win-backs), rather than just writing one-off promotional campaigns. You know how to nurture a lead over time.

A strong foundation in A/B testing mechanics — comfortable formulating clear copy hypotheses, understanding sample size requirements, and knowing when a test result has achieved true statistical significance.

The balance of empathy and compliance: a proven ability to write about highly sensitive personal health topics (menopause symptoms, hormonal changes, wellness) with profound empathy while strictly adhering to healthcare compliance rules and ad-network medical restrictions.

#159739. Tech Report: Bing’s AI Cites Support Pages, PDFs & Staff Bios – 883,313 Citations Analyzed via @sejournal, @dodgejd

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2818 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Bing’s AI Cites Support Pages, PDFs & Staff Bios – 883,313 Citations Analyzed via @sejournal, @dodgejd

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In February, Bing rolled out the public preview of its AI Performance Reporting function inside Webmaster Tools.
  • Blog posts, product pages, and homepages account for less than half of the citations in our sample, 42% combined.
  • The single most cited URL in our data set was an app page for a consumer product with an integrated mobile app component.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In February, Bing rolled out the public preview of its AI Performance Reporting function inside Webmaster Tools. Since then, we have been using it to gauge a bit more insight into what Bing is citing and what might be impacting those results. Monitoring different sites since then, we set out to analyze more than 883,000 AI citations across 26 brands, which surfaced a few things that may surprise you.

Blog posts, product pages, and homepages account for less than half of the citations in our sample, 42% combined. The other 58% is a mix of app pages, attractions lists, instruction manuals, course catalogs, key personnel directors, and PDFs that nobody on a content team was likely thinking about.

The single most cited URL in our data set was an app page for a consumer product with an integrated mobile app component. The second was an attractions list for a tourism destination organization.

There certainly are other tools out there at the disposal of SEOs that help us understand what AI citations might look like, but at the time, this data was reported out of the only first-party tool inside of a search engine to do so. As soon as access was provided in February, we pulled AI reports for 15 different brands and published our findings. Since then, Microsoft has added query-to-page mapping, intent and topic labels, Citation Share, and a Topics Portfolio beta. They have also backfilled much of the underlying data from previous months’ releases, allowing us to pull data for the same 15 brands, plus an additional batch to spot any gaps or trends.

Recent findings suggest that understanding semantic differences between searchers and the fact that all of the data inside the AI Reporting is sampled to some extent, we started with the page-level reporting instead of queries. Across most sites, the pages export will provide you with a broader data set to work from, also moving you past the common practitioner question, which is “what are people prompting,” when we set out to try and better understand “what on my site does the machine actually use?”.

Industry observers note that we explored the AI reports from 26 different brands across nine verticals. Included were destination marketing organizations, resorts and hoteliers, ecommerce brands, B2B manufacturers, colleges and universities, an EdTech platform, regional healthcare providers, government-adjacent business services, and a financial institution.

Sources indicate that inside the AI Reporting portion, we exported the three report views for each brand: Grounding Queries, Cited Pages, and the Daily Overview. By the numbers, our overview totals delivered over 1.1 million citations across the brands, with over 883,000 on 10,861 URLs and a grounding query export of nearly 300,000 citations across 2,797 queries.

Grounding queries are the search phrases Microsoft’s AI generates to retrieve content, not the words people type, and Microsoft states grounding query data “represents a sample of overall citation activity.” Pulling data from the fall highlights us how much of a sample. Meaning that for every brand we reviewed, the query export sums to between 5% and 39% of the overview total, and the page export is between 63% and 100%. That is why we used page counts rather than queries for pattern spotting.

It has been revealed that two additional rules were held in the course of our analysis. First, no raw-count comparisons were used across the periods. Knowing Microsoft backfilled AI Performance data from June 1, 2026, Krishna Madhavan described the resulting jumps as “just regular data backfilling” on X. Second, the two data pulls cover different seasons, and we only carried forward the findings that held up across both, spring and fall, and set aside the ones that seasonality could explain.

See also: Microsoft Clarity Now Shows Grounding Queries Behind AI Citations.

Across all 883,313 page citations, grouped by what the page is for:.

As one might expect, pooled numbers are leaning toward big sites, and the median brand across the data looks quite different. Product and service pages accounted for 32%, whereas editorial content was 15%, homepage 8%, and everything else thereafter was much smaller.

Citations appear to be fairly concentrated. Across the whole set, just over 2% of the URLs carry half of all citations. Breaking this down even more, we noted that it takes 1,441 URLs in our data to reach 80%. For a typical brand, the top page alone accounts for 12.7% of its citations and takes about 40 pages to reach 80% citation volume. As conversational search continues to grow, SEOs understand that the long-tail queries are expanding, but most of what Bing’s AI pulls from is a handful of pages.

Recent findings suggest that across destination marketing organization websites, events and things-to-do pages remain nearly 50% of the citations, and listing directories make up another 15%, with lodging-related pages falling in at under 1%. The single biggest anomaly that stood out was a tourism attraction list with nearly 17,000 citations. Grounding queries are highly seasonal, with major events and festivals delivering a large share of the citations. What does this mean for destination marketers? The sites are highly sought after and relied upon for things to do, see, and experience, though less likely for the actual places to stay.

Wanting to explore more lodging-oriented searches, we added in additional resort and hotelier properties where heads in beds is a primary function of their business. Lodging and reservations pages account for 4.3% of citations across resorts, wherein activities-related content such as golf, ski, dining, and packages pages account for nearly 50% of the citations. While one resort was cited for instructional content around golf techniques, regional golf trips were more likely to garner the results that generate positive conversations in the boardroom. What does this mean for resorts and hoteliers? Monitoring these trends over the course of a season, be it summer or winter, allows a resort to see the activity mix that rotates with the calendar. It’s worth noting that a resort (not a hotel) is cited as a place that does something, and almost never as just a place to sleep.

No surprise to anyone developing SEO strategies for ecommerce brands, product and category pages account for 40% of the citations, with support and documentation-related pages residing at 26%, and specific app/login pages making up nearly 20% of the citations. Stripping out the one brand whose app page is the most cited URL in our study, the product pages rise to 64% of the citations. A second brand that pairs a physical product with an app and a service blueprint indicates the same shape. Its service plan and product support pages are two of its top three cited URLs, and PDF instruction manuals sit in its top 10. For brands that are focused on the growth of their app-enabled products, this means reviewing how you are positioned to own the support conversation. Similar to traditional search, AI models appear to be just fine citing your PDF documents, which leads to a poor customer experience and puts you down a path of hard-to-update legacy content.

The closer a B2B brand is to the solution being delivered, the better. Across the brands reviewed, editorial content accounted for 46% of the citations. At one manufacturing services brand with a global presence, over 70% of the citations were URLs from technical how-to articles. The same can be said for training and tutorial-based content, especially video libraries, which accounted for 73% of citations. The exception to that is a product manufacturer whose catalog pages account for over 70% of the citations and another 10% for product literature PDFs. Meaning, if you are in the business of making highly specialized and technical products, the machine is just as happy sourcing its answers from a PDF, though again it causes more friction on the side of the customer and content teams who have to manage legacy updates over time.

Industry observers note that academic programs, admissions-related pages, and financial aid make up nearly 40% of the citations for the higher ed vertical. From there, it filters out into reference material and course handouts at 13%; support and IT-related pages also at 13%; editorial articles come in at 12%, with faculty and about pages at 11%. For colleges and universities, the bulk of the pages being cited fall into more of an information-gathering category around what courses are offered, when, and the financial implications. For those working in academia, specifically higher ed, reviewing which of your pages are being referenced the most should start to provide you with insights on what your audience is seeking. If you’re a university that’s built on research and studies, there are clear signals that optimizing who your people are is a critical step that is potentially overlooked.

Across the verticals reviewed, three categories surfaced that no content calendar is at the moment accounting for, and why would it? Noting PDF documents account for over 6% of all citations in total. Within the EdTech platform we reviewed, they account for nearly 17% of citations, with course catalogs also following a similar trend. Within one university, PDFs were 11% of their citations, surfacing elements from not just the course catalog but also core requirements that students need by program. Certainly, if you’re looking to own more of the conversation around your programs and what students can expect vs. letting the AI base it off of outdated PDFs, this is a prime opportunity to take action.

Industry observers note that at one ecommerce brand, PDFs were 10.4% of all citations, all of them instruction manuals. This serves as a reminder that if a PDF is the best document you have on a subject, it could very well be cited as the best document you have on the matter itself. For brands with products that require technical support, while revising a single PDF might seem like the approach to take, consider how many PDF documents are residing in your CMS that are outdated vs. placing the actual helpful information in an HTML format on your site.

The homepages of many websites don’t go unnoticed in our review. Homepages are 6.8% of all citations pooled, and the homepage is the single most cited page for nine of the 26 brands reviewed. When nothing else on a site carries deeper insights about the brand, its services or products, the homepage is carrying a much higher share of the citations. It doesn’t matter the size of the brand either; that’s a signal that is worth reviewing to help you determine what the AI is thinking about your brand.

Across healthcare, education, and EdTech, people and about pages carry between 4% and 11% of citations by vertical, and 18% at one university. When the AI answer is related to who you are as a brand or an individual, where you are located, and the key individuals who work there, these pages become critical elements when directing the LLMs. How many of these page types get published once, only to never be revisited and kept up to date?

Looking back to an early study we did on the insights on what Bing’s Webmaster Tools was telling us about AI Citations, we revisited 15 of the original brands to determine what shifted over the course of time. Most of what moved was seasonal, and based on that, we decided to leave those elements out. However, we did find three areas worth investigating further.

Sources indicate that in our original review in February, login, portal, and sign-in queries accounted for approximately 18% of all citations across the brands. In the fall window, that shrunk to just above 1%.

According to recent reports, within the higher education sector, 45% of the citations originally came from login and portal queries. As we observed this shift into the fall, the same number of grounding queries had dropped to just shy of 1%. Login queries for the EdTech brand also dropped from 17% to less than 1%. And while there certainly is the seasonal argument to be made, we can look at August through October as being key times at most universities and colleges as the start of a semester. We expect institutional login lookups to increase around that time, and in fact, they did not.

In a recent development, product support for the ecommerce brands went the other direction, with one brand’s support and access-related content rising from 17% to 42% of its citations. Noting that fall is the peak season for the brand and that demand is trending exactly where you might expect it to be.

Bing’s June patch added intent labels to the reporting, with Navigational among them. The February login queries are exactly what that label would catch. It also would appear that Microsoft has not mentioned it suppresses AI answers differently across intent types, and what we are describing is more of a pattern to spot and not a mechanism within the report.

Recent findings suggest that for the median brand, only 37% of the citations found in our February review came from query strings that still appear in the fall export, and that is before accounting for any seasonal shifts. Across each of the brand’s top ten queries this spring, we note that approximately 56% are completely absent from the fall data pull. If your brand operates around any cyclicality where it is impacted by major events, holidays, or even seasonal activities, that explains some of the difference but not all.

Across the original data pull in February, we found a handful of location-only queries. Those that included [events near me], [concerts near me], and [holiday events near me], without a destination even in the query string, were present. Revisiting the same brands this fall, we see that the near me query left the data. Noting many of the AI-generated search results are favoring sites such as Eventbrite, Ticketmaster, and similar aggregator sites. The more local and regional focused your brand is, such as a multi-location storefront, the location-based data is going to be stronger and likely in line with what you experience in traditional search.

We continue to see branded searches spread into the AI Overviews in Google, yet the data coming out of Google is still not as detailed as we would like. Within Bing, we do get a view into Citation Shares, which was added in June. This reports on the percentage of citations your site receives out of all citations shown for a grounding query, which should help you determine how much of the answer your brand actually holds.

Citation Share is Bing’s measure of how much of an answer your site has supplied. For each grounding query, it reports what percentage of all citations shown for that query pointed to your pages. On branded queries, the sites in our analysis supplied 67% of the citations, and other sites supplied 33%. On non-branded queries, the sites supplied 25% and other sites supplied 75%. Compare this to your traditional search results and determine how much your branded searches are triggering AI-generated results.

Non-branded searches tend to always be the opportunity in traditional search, and AI-generated results are certainly no different. The data in our most recent series of exports confirms this. On a non-branded query, three of every four citations are going to someone else.

According to recent reports, up front, know that the data is all sampled, but likely the best we have to work with at the moment. The pipeline is constantly backfilling, so an increase across a three-month time period could indicate more usage, more backfill on recent dates, or both. Right now, the recommendation is to use the data as a guide and report on what the dashboard highlights rather than calling it growth.

Recent findings suggest that overall, Bing’s intent labels hold up well, though it could be argued that their topic labels do not yet. Our review highlighted one consumer product brand filed under “Home Security Systems” for 57% of its citations. Microsoft’s June post allows that labels “may be broad” for niche domains, so initiative on re-sorting them yourself. It’s also worth noting that not every grounding query traces back to a person. Queries of seven or more words grew from 1% of citations in February to 3% this fall, and some of them are plainly monitoring tools running on a schedule. Citation counts in any tool will include machine-initiated queries, and no report separates those out right now.

Recent findings suggest that while Google remains the top in regards to search volume, the data coming out of their AI insights reporting is lackluster. Bing remains one of the better sources for a site owner to gauge first-party insights on what gets cited. Just be sure you read it for what it is: a sampling of your brand’s data. According to recent reports, right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each manufacturer’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft noted they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”.

Industry observers note that anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI states it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an notable step,” writing in a tweet that the tech giant supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”.

Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

“Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres said. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”.

Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

To reach newly introduced audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

Recent findings suggest that from the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

“The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is presently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

It has been revealed that another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres noted. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”.

In a recent development, not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

In a recent development, “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”.

CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

“We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he noted. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”.

Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

Recent findings suggest that RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler mentioned. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”.

Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.).

Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler noted. Only 21% were “doom only.”.

In a recent development, the video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

Sources indicate that “We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres mentioned. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”.

What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler remarked.).

Industry observers note that “I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler said. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”.

It has been revealed that part of the problem, he said, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that google’s November 2026 core update finished rolling out on Nov. 24, according to the Search Status Dashboard, putting the first post-update week Google suggests comparing in Search Console on U.S. Thanksgiving, Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

In a recent development, the dashboard’s latest entry, posted at 6:03 a.m. PT, reads: “The rollout was complete as of November 24, 2026.” The upgrade began rolling out Nov. 10, so it finished inside the two-week window Google gave at launch, which I covered that day.

Glenn Gabe, SEO and AI Search Consultant at G-Squared Interactive, dates the enhancement’s impact to Nov. 13, three days after the rollout began. In a Nov. 17 post on X, he wrote that he believed the update “landed on Friday the 13th,” with Search Console showing major surges and drops for affected sites starting that day.

Sources indicate that gabe leaned on Search Console because third-party SEO tools were “all over the place due to poisoning, filtering, etc.” By Nov. 20, he said the tools’ trend lines matched what he saw in Search Console for those sites.

Recent findings suggest that lily Ray, Founder of Algorythmic and VP, SEO & AI Search at Amsive, shared a chart on LinkedIn on Nov. 23 showing subfolders and subdomains on six sites that “have been dropping fast since Google’s November core upgrade started.” Each folder held one template repeated thousands of times, such as a page per word, per area code or per “X vs Y” word pairing. She wrote that most of the folders target searches “not closely related to the business offering.”.

According to recent reports, ray wrote that within each site, “the content section (blog, resources, etc.) is falling hard while the main product/brand pages stay strong.” She has seen AI Overview and AI Mode citations to those folders “show similar drops” too. Her chart uses SISTRIX visibility data, with the same trend lines checked in Ahrefs, and doesn’t name the sites.

Sources indicate that ray called these “new examples of the exact same SEO problems that have been hurting sites during core updates for years.” In an Oct. 7 column for SEJ, she listed templated, programmatic pages among the patterns she’d found on sites hit by Google updates this year.

According to recent reports, google’s recommendations for core updates suggest waiting until at least a full week after an patch has finished rolling out, then trying to compare a week of data post-rollout, Nov. 25 to Dec. 1 on this update’s dates, to a week of data pre-rollout such as Nov. 3-9.

For retail sites, the week prior to the rollout will include regular traffic while the week immediately following the rollout includes Black Friday and may reflect holiday traffic. Another check would be comparing the same holiday traffic from last year alongside Google’s suggested comparative week.

Marie Haynes wrote for SEJ that the click spike some site owners were seeing in their Search Console from Oct. 31-Nov. 2 wasn’t human traffic. A baseline start date of Nov. 3 excludes those days. There is also a logging glitch listed on Google’s data anomalies page that resulted in lower impression counts in the Generative AI performance report for Nov. 9-11, which coincides with the end of the baseline week.

Sources indicate that using a page path filter in the Performance report allows you to isolate your product pages and compare these to a templated content folder as described by Ray. Google’s guidance also says to avoid making changes to content that’s already performing well.

Sources indicate that the first full week after completion ends Dec. 1, so the comparison Google suggests can run once that day’s data reaches Search Console. Gabe wrote on Nov. 20 that tremors and reversals “can always happen as Google updates additional core systems” or spots something off in its results after an enhancement.

College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

According to recent reports, but this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.).

On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins confirmed the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:.

The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

But we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM.

Sources indicate that for those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one tech giant or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

Indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The Latest York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.).

Collins says The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the Upcoming Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently mentioned no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.).

So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The Latest Orleans Bowl.

According to recent reports, I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM.

Then the folks who run the Latest Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our prepares to highlight our mascot:.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM.

Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in New Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and mentioned it straight up: "No.".

We asked why. They noted politics. And the Sickos Guy.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM.

While the Upcoming Orleans Bowl might be out, several currently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • WordPress is in use on 38.4% of all websites, according to W3Techs, Nov.
  • Shopify improved 0.6 points over the year; Wix and Squarespace barely changed.
  • It has been revealed that there are more than 20 million websites included in W3Techs’ survey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WordPress is in use on 38.4% of all websites, according to W3Techs, Nov. 23. A year prior, WordPress was being used on 43.2% of all websites. In that time, the share of websites using none of the content management systems tracked by W3Techs grew 4.4 percentage points, from 28.6% to 33.0%.

Shopify improved 0.6 points over the year; Wix and Squarespace barely changed. For sites with no detected CMS, neither a WordPress SEO plugin nor another platform’s defaults can be assumed to handle titles, canonical tags and sitemaps.

It has been revealed that there are more than 20 million websites included in W3Techs’ survey. The data is updated each day. Shelley Walsh’s November CMS market share upgrade used the survey’s Nov. 13 figures. At that time, WordPress had dropped to 39.2% of all websites.

WordPress’s percentage of all sites has fallen 1.1 points so far in November, which is larger than its fall in any single complete month this year, per the survey’s month-by-month data.

It has been revealed that wordPress’ declines have been larger since August. For the first seven months of the year, WordPress fell less than 0.5 points each month. It then dropped 0.5 points a month in August and September, and 0.7 points in October.

Roger Montti reported that WordPress fell for the sixth consecutive month as of May, when it was at 41.9%.

The gap between WordPress and sites with no detected CMS narrowed from 14.6 percentage points to 5.4 points over the period shown below.

WordPress Fell As The Share With No Detected CMS Rose.

Share of all websites in W3Techs’ survey, Nov. 1, 2025 to Nov. 23, 2026.

WordPress fell 4.8 points over the year. Shopify rose from 4.9% to 5.5% of all websites and Wix from 4.1% to 4.2%, while Squarespace held steady and Joomla and Drupal slipped. The share of sites with no detected CMS rose 4.4 points over the same year.

Sources indicate that wix grows on the survey’s market share measure, which counts only sites with a CMS W3Techs detects. That pool gets smaller as the share with no detected CMS grows. By that count, WordPress fell from 60.5% to 57.3%, while Wix rose from 5.7% to 6.2% and Shopify rose too. Most of Wix’s gain comes from the smaller pool, since its share of all websites barely changed.

In a recent development, in March, I noted that the share of sites with no detected CMS stood at 28.9%, close to its low after years of decline. Since February, it has risen each month.

Industry observers note that W3Techs now lists Lovable as a CMS, describing it as “an AI-powered platform for building websites”. It lists Lovable at 0.5% of total websites, about 0.1 point below Drupal’s current 0.6%.

The monthly table provided by W3Techs does not show any Lovable data prior to November.

Recent findings suggest that in her report, Shelley said that she is most interested in how AI and vibecoding may influence CMS platforms, and whether there will be more non-CMS based websites. Now that W3Techs has Lovable on its list, her first question has a number, at least for one AI builder.

Industry observers note that nearly one-third of websites in W3Techs’ survey are now using none of the CMSs it tracks. That means you can’t count on a WordPress SEO plugin, or another platform’s defaults, to set or manage title tags, canonical tags, robots meta directives, or sitemaps on such websites. An audit or pitch will need to determine what handles them on these websites, or if nothing does.

The key figure to keep an eye on is the share of sites running none of the CMSs tracked by W3Techs, which has risen 1.5 points since Oct. 1. The Dec. 1 numbers will help show whether that pace continues.

“I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”.

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

For Nikita Redkar, a significant part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

According to recent reports, in a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around Newly introduced York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

“I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar noted. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”.

Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Recent findings suggest that hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. In a recent development, tameez: Tell me about why this work is important to you. Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

Sources indicate that for one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have remarked this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

Redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

That’s just the reality; people are on social media, everyone’s attention span is shot, which sucks. We could try to fix that, but at this moment, we’re not fixing it. It’s really helpful to go on social media and talk [about your reporting] because journalists work hard on their articles.

It has been revealed that creators [should] take more time. We rush way too much. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that clutch builds AI agents that work on behalf of credit unions.
  • As a FDE you are one of the two engineers on an agent.
  • Sources indicate that this is a senior engineering role, not a solutions or support role.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that clutch builds AI agents that work on behalf of credit unions. Emma, our collections agent, is live at five credit unions and handled 60,000+ member conversations in her first twelve weeks at one of them. Behind her is a growing portfolio: origination, fraud step-up, member (re)engagement and activation agents, all built on the same Agents Platform (TypeScript, NestJS, our own agent SDK, MCP, Temporal, promptfoo).

As a FDE you are one of the two engineers on an agent. You take it from "sold" to "live and performing" at a specific credit union: you sit in the discovery sessions, you build the integrations to their core banking and loan systems, you author and tune the agent's behavior, you run the live tests with their staff, and you stay with it through go-live and the first weeks of production. When something needs a person in the room, you are the one who flies.

Sources indicate that this is a senior engineering role, not a solutions or support role. You write production code in our monorepo every week: integrations, modules, and the agents themselves (prompts, tools, evals), together with the other engineers on the pod. The difference from a traditional engineer is that you are on site more often, you make judgment calls in front of the customer, and you own the outcome. What you learn in the field flows straight back into the product: defaults, playbooks, and the platform capabilities the next agent will need.

Recent findings suggest that you build; our AI Operations Managers deliver. The pod (pod lead plus engineers) designs and builds each agent in a high-touch way with the first customers. Once the agent is defined and live, AI Ops coordinates the implementations, configuration and ongoing success at the next credit unions. You hand them something that works and a playbook to run it.

Sources indicate that this role requires roughly 20% of travel on average, with one- to two-week stretches around kickoffs and go-lives. Based in the US, able to travel on short notice.

Recent findings suggest that you'll join the Agents team, a small, senior group operating as a startup inside Clutch: seven engineers, a dedicated AI product group, and AI sales specialists, working directly with some of the largest credit unions in the country. Every agent is staffed by a pair of engineers, one leaning toward the conversation and LLM side, one toward software and integrations, with a pod lead who owns the product day to day. There is no layer between you and the customer, and no layer between you and the platform team.

Industry observers note that the operating style is direct, written, and evidence-driven: BLUF updates, evals over opinions, business outcomes over ticket counts. The team is spread across Brazil, Argentina and the US and works async by default. Being on site is a tool we use at specific moments (kickoff, live testing, go-live), not a permanent posting.

Ship your first production change to a live agent through the team's review process, and be able to explain how a member's call flows through the Agents Platform end to end.

Learn one agent deeply: system prompt, tool contracts, orchestration triggers, compliance gates, and the implementation process from kickoff to go-live.

Join at least one credit union implementation as the second engineer, including a live testing session with their staff.

Map where the current implementation process loses time and where a default or a tool would have removed a round trip.

Own the technical side of one credit union implementation end to end: core and LOS integration, agent configuration, testing, go-live, and the first weeks of production.

Run the eval and tuning loop for your agent (golden transcripts, rubric judges, regression suite) and be trusted to change its behavior without a second engineer checking your work.

Have completed at least two on-site visits and turned what you heard there into product decisions with your pod lead and PM.

Contribute at least one reusable capability back to the Agents Platform that the next implementation will not have to rebuild.

Have taken one net-newly introduced agent from sold to live at its first credit union, with data you can show the partner.

Be the engineer credit union staff ask for by name when something in their deployment needs to change.

Have written the implementation playbook for your agent well enough that the AI Ops team runs the second and third credit union without you.

Be shaping what the next agents look like, because you have seen where the current ones break in the field.

Industry observers note that 7+ years of software engineering in a fast-paced environment, preferably in SaaS and/or Fintech, with senior TypeScript and Node.js backend experience in a large codebase (NestJS, CQRS, schema-validated boundaries, dependency injection). We do not count years of AI experience; the field is too young for that to mean anything. We look at what you have shipped and how you reason about it.

Integration and API engineering: secure service-to-service endpoints, third-party APIs, webhooks, and the patience to work with legacy banking systems that were not designed to be integrated.

According to recent reports, security and auth judgment: OAuth and machine-to-machine auth, tenant-scoped access, secrets handling, no PII in logs. Our agents touch sensitive member data and operate under consumer-contact regulation.

It has been revealed that customer presence: you can sit across from a VP of Collections, hear a request, and say "here is what I recommend and why", including when the answer is no. You are comfortable making calls in the room and owning them afterwards.

Code-quality judgment under deadline pressure: you take on debt deliberately, name it, and pay it down, rather than gold-plating or leaving silent debt behind.

Genuine appetite for LLM agents: eval discipline for non-deterministic systems, reading a system prompt like code, understanding that some decisions must never reach the model. Curiosity plus shipped work is enough; research depth is not required.

Nice to have, explicitly not required: voice and telephony (LiveKit, Twilio), Temporal or event-driven orchestration, Python, core banking or LOS integration experience, credit union or banking domain knowledge.

Remote Flexibility: Enjoy the freedom of remote work from anywhere, balancing life and career seamlessly.

Unforgettable Off-Sites: Twice a year, bond with colleagues in exciting destinations, fostering teamwork and fresh ideas.

Paid Time Off: Enjoy flexible PTO days yearly for relaxation and rejuvenation.

Stock Options: Joining us means having a stake in our success, so you'll receive stock options as part of your compensation package.

Home Office Setup: Create your ideal workspace with a dedicated budget for home office essentials.

Work Trip Budget: Grow personally and professionally with a budget for work-related trips and co-working.

Health Coverage: Prioritize your well-being with comprehensive health and dental insurance intends.

Clutch is a revolutionary vertical SaaS organization, proudly backed by Andreessen Horowitz (A16z), aimed at revolutionizing the way Credit Unions engage and change the lives of their members. As a champion of financial well-being, we address the urgent need for affordable lending solutions in an era where the average American grapples with over $155,000 in household debt. Unlike traditional financial institutions, Clutch develops software to turn Credit Unions into FinTech lenders and leverage their balance sheets to responsibly lend to over 130M Americans. Our mission extends beyond mere financial transactions; we strive to fundamentally enhance the way credit unions interact with their members. By integrating cutting-edge technologies and user-centric designs, we help credit unions provide seamless digital experiences that are on par with leading tech companies. This approach not only preserves but revitalizes the longstanding tradition of community and member-focused service inherent to credit unions.

Sources indicate that clutch is an equal opportunity employer. All applicants will be considered for employment without attention to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, veteran or disability status.

Base salary does not include bonus, equity, or benefits, which are offered in addition as applicable.Applications will be accepted on an ongoing basis.

“We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”.

Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the organization to scrape the websites of Meta Business account customers.

On Thursday, the tech giant took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an upgrade to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”.

It has been revealed that meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms revision. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”.

Since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the organization was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”.

In the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.
