💡 Key Takeaways
  • LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing.
  • In a recent development, the Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit is the technical owner and architect of the systems that power our go-to-market engine.
  • Salesforce is our system of record for revenue, pipeline, and customer data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

In a recent development, the Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit is the technical owner and architect of the systems that power our go-to-market engine. You'll decide how our GTM stack is designed, what we build versus buy, and where we invest next — and you'll be hands-on building it: Salesforce architecture, integrations, enrichment pipelines, and the agentic workflows that help Sales and Marketing move faster and smarter.

Salesforce is our system of record for revenue, pipeline, and customer data. HubSpot is our marketing layer for campaigns and lead generation, and what it captures needs to flow cleanly and reliably into Salesforce. Around them sits a growing stack of enrichment, sales intelligence, billing, and data platform tools. You'll own the architecture that ties it all together: disciplined change management, observable pipelines, data models built for AI consumption, and agentic workflows that act on GTM signals at scale — designed to serve the business for years, not quarters.

Industry observers note that this role sits at the intersection of GTM, Data, Finance, and Engineering. You'll work directly with senior leaders to shape the GTM systems roadmap, turn business strategy into technical looks, and guide decisions that span multiple teams. You'll also help grow the engineers around you, setting the technical standards and practices the team builds on.

In a recent development, you understand the difference between owning a system and gatekeeping one. Sales lives in Salesforce. Marketing lives in HubSpot. Your job is to make sure both are governed well enough that others can work in them effectively, and powerful enough that the GTM team can do things they couldn't do before.

You'll thrive as a Staff GTM Systems Engineer if you:.

Are known as the go-to person for tough technical problems, and have good judgment about which ones matter most.

Think in systems and long time horizons, and can make confident architectural decisions with incomplete information.

Can clearly explain complex technical concepts and tradeoffs to engineers and executives alike.

Believe systems should be managed with engineering discipline.

Ship fast and reliably — your work holds up in production.

Are a fast learner, frequently picking up fresh languages and tools.

Find real satisfaction in mentoring other engineers and helping them grow.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google announced its December 2026 core revision on the Search Status Dashboard today, before the rollout, and said what the update is meant to improve.

  • PT, approximately an hour after Google posted that the November core update was complete.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google announced its December 2026 core revision on the Search Status Dashboard today, before the rollout, and said what the update is meant to improve. The entry states it focuses on how Google’s systems understand and rank relevant content, including for longer and more complex questions. It’s also meant to improve personalized results for people who have personalization turned on.

The entry gives no set time for this upcoming enhancement, but it has been scheduled for sometime in December. It also does not provide information on how long the rollout of the update will last.

It appeared at 7:03 a.m. PT, approximately an hour after Google posted that the November core update was complete. Sites that are still reviewing their results from the November core update can expect another core update within weeks of the last one ending.

“Preannounced the December 2026 core upgrade, which focuses on multiple improvements to how our systems understand and rank relevant content (including for longer and more complex questions), as well as improving personalized results for people who have personalization turned on. This core update applies to all locations and languages where Google Search is available, and our guidance about general core updates applies. This update is scheduled to be released in December 2026.”.

According to recent reports, google provides information about how different people can get different results. A person’s Google Account information, such as their Search Services History, can influence what they see in search results. However, personalized search does not change every result returned for a query. Instead, it may change the order of individual results or entire result groups (for example, videos may appear before web links for someone who has historically preferred videos).

According to recent reports, google’s entries for this year’s March, May and November core updates gave a rollout window, and November’s added the revision’s scope. None of the three said what its update focused on.

It has been revealed that in June 2019, Google’s SearchLiaison account on Twitter announced the June 2019 core update the day before it was released, as my colleague Roger Montti reported. This December notice comes at least a week before the rollout.

The December release window is close enough to November’s core update rollout end date that there may be little time to test the effects of the previous month’s algorithmic changes prior to the next update.

Google’s core revision webpage advises people to wait at least seven days after an update concludes, then compare that week with a week preceding the rollout’s initiation.

According to recent reports, the first full week following the completion of November’s core update would run from Nov. 25 through Dec. 1. This is a period that includes U.S. Thanksgiving, Black Friday and Cyber Monday, an overlap I pointed out when November’s rollout started. The December rollout could begin as early as Dec. 1, the final day of that week, and any week after it begins may reflect both updates.

It has been revealed that search Console’s custom annotations can mark Nov. 24, when November’s update finished, and December’s start date once it’s known.

When the December rollout starts, its start date closes the gap between the two revealed updates. We’ll cover the rollout then.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

According to recent reports, A upcoming study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

If there’s one major takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

Industry observers note that A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less important — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

That truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

Industry observers note that J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

Participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how notable the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty new. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a big gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

#159715. A Billboard CEO Notes AI Makes Ads Cheaper, Not Better – 3 Tests For Google Ads via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

A Billboard CEO Notes AI Makes Ads Cheaper, Not Better – 3 Tests For Google Ads via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chris Grosso runs a company that sells ads on sidewalk kiosks, and he just gave me the most useful warning I’ve heard this year about AI in paid media.
  • According to recent reports, that sentence should make anyone running Performance Max, AI Max, or Smart Bidding a little uncomfortable.
  • Grosso’s industry never had a click to hide behind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chris Grosso runs a company that sells ads on sidewalk kiosks, and he just gave me the most useful warning I’ve heard this year about AI in paid media. “For now, AI is about efficiency more than effectiveness,” the CEO of Intersection, the out-of-home media company behind LinkNYC, told me by email.

According to recent reports, that sentence should make anyone running Performance Max, AI Max, or Smart Bidding a little uncomfortable. AI is plainly making media cheaper and faster to plan and buy. Whether it makes the plan better is a separate question, and most Google Ads accounts aren’t set up to answer it.

Grosso’s industry never had a click to hide behind. Out-of-home had to prove its value with holdout groups, foot traffic, and brand lift long before search marketers worried about zero-click results. Below is what he told me, why it matters to people who live in Google Ads, and three tests you can set up before Q1 budgets lock.

The timing of this conversation isn’t an accident. Anthropic’s S-1, filed Oct. 26, reveals its advertising spend rising from $33 million in 2024 to $147 million in 2025, according to Digiday’s reading of the filing. The S-1 attributes the increase to higher media and PR spending around product launches.

Recent findings suggest that AI companies are no longer just building the tools that buy ads. They have become sizable advertisers themselves, and launch-driven brand spending is exactly the kind of money that last-click attribution struggles to credit.

It has been revealed that the buying side is changing too. More than 10% of Intersection’s business is now transacted programmatically, Grosso told me, and that share is growing fast. His read is that demand-side platforms are using AI to optimize campaigns, and that out-of-home is absorbing demand that used to go to the open web, “where AI is eroding the model.”.

In a recent development, that’s a seller’s view, and Intersection benefits if buyers share it. But if he’s right, the budget you park in Google Network inventory has a fresh competitor on the street corner.

Recent findings suggest that intersection also opened its order management system to AI assistants in May. Its press release states agencies and brands can now plan and reserve campaigns on more than 7,000 digital screens through Claude and ChatGPT, using a Model Context Protocol connection built on IAB Tech Lab’s OpenDirect 2.0 specification.

When a media planner can price a LinkNYC flight in the same chat window where they draft a Search budget, every channel gets judged side-by-side. Your Google Ads numbers will need to hold up in that comparison.

See also: How Much Of Your Paid Media Budget Should Be Allocated To Upper Funnel?

In a recent development, grosso’s method is one most PPC managers know in theory and rarely run in practice. Intersection splits audiences into people who were exposed to a campaign and people who weren’t, then compares the lift between the two groups.

“It doesn’t matter whether the person went on to use an AI assistant or a search engine,” he mentioned. When a pixel fires, the digital event is matched back to the exposed group. For retail clients, the comparison is foot traffic, meaning whether exposed devices were more likely to enter a geofence.

Then he said something I wish more search marketers would say out loud. “Causation is harder to prove. Did a search ad cause someone to click, or did years of branding do it?”.

He’s describing your branded Search campaign.

Branded keywords routinely post the best ROAS in an account because they harvest demand that other channels created. Smart Bidding sees those conversions, values them, and bids to win more of them. Nothing in the platform’s attribution report tells you how many of those buyers would have arrived anyway.

Industry observers note that grosso’s measurement partners are also trying to follow consumers into AI assistants. One of Intersection’s brand survey partners, he told me, has built an AI-assistant product integrated with ChatGPT and Gemini that collects 2.35 million unique AI conversations every 30 days. For a new meal launching at a major fast-food chain, that kind of study can show whether people exposed to the out-of-home campaign later visited the chain, and whether they searched for the new meal through AI channels during the flight.

“This doesn’t solve for last touch,” Grosso noted, “but it’s one step closer to providing visibility into the user’s journey.” That’s a more honest claim than most attribution vendors make.

See also: How To Measure Brand Marketing Efforts (And Prove Their ROI).

Grosso told me AI removes friction from buying out-of-home, one of advertising’s most fragmented marketplaces, so advertisers “can do a lot more OOH, faster.” He did not claim AI makes those campaigns work better.

I think he’s right, and I think the same distinction applies inside Google Ads.

According to recent reports, performance Max and AI Max save time. They consolidate campaigns, generate asset variations, and find queries a human wouldn’t have added. Those are efficiency gains. Effectiveness is a bigger claim, because it means the same dollars produced more incremental sales than the old setup would have. Google’s published performance figures for its AI campaign types are Google’s claims, measured by Google, and an advertiser who wants to know whether they hold in their own account has to test them.

Grosso also warned against speed for its own sake. “Quick research outcomes don’t always equate to high-quality, representative data,” he said. He advises CMOs to set core metrics and watch them over sustained periods, because narrow dollar-for-dollar justification risks missing long-term growth and brand building.

Industry observers note that he measures at three levels. The first is reach and frequency, for the channel and incrementally across the whole media initiative. The second is consideration signals such as website and store visits. The third is actual transactions. Most PPC dashboards jump straight to the third level and treat the conversions column as proof.

See also: Is Performance Max Actually Better Than Running Separate Campaigns? – Ask A PPC.

In a recent development, out-of-home is rebuilding its own currency. On March 31, 2026, Geopath and the OAAA selected Ipsos to run a pilot of a next-generation audience measurement system in the second half of the year. Grosso, whose company notes he sits on the boards of both organizations, called the pilot a major development.

Today’s approach, he noted, assigns an impression value that is the same no matter the time of year. The pilot is meant to produce an ongoing forecast that planners can compare with other channels.

Search has the opposite problem. Google Ads has abundant, near-real-time data. What it lacks is an independent referee, because the platform that sells the clicks also counts the conversions.

Google has been narrowing that gap with its own experiment tools, and three of them matter here.

That last change deserves a raised eyebrow. Branded query volume is a reasonable signal of demand created by TV, video, or a kiosk on Sixth Avenue. It is also measured on Google’s own surface and used inside a model that helps decide how much to spend on Google. Use it, but don’t let it be the only judge.

Here’s what I would do before Q1 budgets are set.

Sources indicate that test branded Search before you raise its budget. If your account qualifies, run Conversion Lift based on users on your branded Search campaign. If it doesn’t, pause brand ads in a set of matched regions for two to four weeks and compare total brand conversions, paid plus organic, against regions where ads kept running. Hold budget, creative, and bid strategy constant while the test runs, and give it at least two weeks, which is the minimum Google has recommended for lift studies.

Measure your manufacturer’s offline media from inside Google Ads. If your brand buys out-of-home, TV, or radio in specific markets, ask for the flight dates and DMAs. Compare branded search impressions, impression share, and CPCs in exposed and unexposed markets. Then use a geo-based lift test or GeoX to estimate how much of your branded Search volume that media created, and stop letting branded Search take full credit in budget meetings.

Report AI efficiency and AI effectiveness on separate lines. When you move spend into Performance Max or AI Max, track time saved and CPA in one place, and incremental conversions per dollar, or iROAS from a lift study, in another. If the first improves and the second doesn’t, you’ve bought efficiency. That may still be worth paying for. Just don’t call it growth.

Recent findings suggest that paid search spent two decades as the most measurable channel in advertising, and that made a lot of us lazy about causation. Out-of-home never had that luxury. Grosso’s industry learned to prove its value with control groups, foot traffic, and brand signals because there was no click to count.

Industry observers note that search is drifting toward the same conditions. People meet a brand on a sidewalk, ask an AI assistant about it, and convert somewhere else.

My view is that the PPC managers who keep their budgets in 2027 will be the ones who can show incremental results instead of attributed ones. The CEO of a kiosk firm remarked it plainly first. Google Ads practitioners should borrow his playbook.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence. We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning latest ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

According to recent reports, fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote manufacturer. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

We have raised $77M and are backed by Craft Ventures (Tesla, Facebook, Airbnb ), Nexus Venture Partners ( Postman, Apollo.io, MinIO, Druva) and Uncorrelated Ventures ( Redis, Rollbar,  Gradle).

As a Business Operations Associate, you will play a pivotal role in shaping the strategic direction and growth of our firm. This role reports to the VP of Business Operations and comes with the exciting responsibility of advancing critical strategic initiatives. Business Operations serves as the swiss-army knife of the organization - you’ll work on a diverse set of projects and no two weeks will be the same. You will collaborate extensively with colleagues from various departments, including Product, Engineering, GTM, People, and Finance. This role offers unique visibility into a hyper-growth startup, providing the opportunity to shape its trajectory and make a substantial impact.

High Quality Decision Making & Leadership Alignment.

Process Improvements & Efficient Operations.

Recent findings suggest that at Fingerprint, we believe in pay transparency — it's part of how we operate as a distributed, remote-first team. Salaries are based on function, level, and geographic location, benchmarked against similar stage growth companies.

Because this role is open across the United States and can be based anywhere our team members work from, the salary range reflects that geographic breadth: $92,000 - $125,000.

Some example salaries for specific locations are below:.

LA, NY, Boston: $109,000 - $125,000.

Chicago, Dallas: $92,000 - $106,000.

Final offer amounts are determined by multiple factors, including the successful candidate's location, experience, and expertise, and may vary from the amounts listed above.

Industry observers note that due to regulatory and security reasons, there’s a small number of countries where we cannot have Fingerprint teammates based. Additionally, because Fingerprint is an all-remote company and people can join our workforce from almost any country, we do not sponsor visas. Fingerprint teammates need to be authorized to work from their home location.

We are dedicated to creating an inclusive work environment for everyone. We embrace and celebrate the unique experiences, perspectives and cultural backgrounds that each employee brings to our workplace. Fingerprint strives to foster an environment where our employees feel respected, valued and empowered, and our team members are at the forefront in helping us promote and sustain an inclusive workplace. Canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism. The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

It has been revealed that RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks.

A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.).

It has been revealed that “It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.”.

Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”.

Read more in The Tyee’s look at Canadian local news here.

AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
  • Industry observers note that we will never sell your address.
  • Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to .
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

Industry observers note that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

Nearly there — check your email.

Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries mentioned they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”.

It has been revealed that as it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

For our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

The use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries said they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

Despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) remarked they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

Our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more swiftly.

According to recent reports, “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) stated they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

Recent findings suggest that using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

Industry observers note that many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

Sources indicate that at the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) said they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

It has been revealed that as in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

It has been revealed that people across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

This also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

Our findings raise several vital questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

It has been revealed that first, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also highlights that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

Sources indicate that third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

The differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a newly introduced dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily consumers and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

Industry observers note that this doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

Recent findings suggest that A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:.

In a recent development, as pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and new hybrid work schedules.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday, I spent time looking for the local news outlets that have foregone or reduced office space and opted for primarily remote work in recent years. Here are some:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that according to a latest ranking section released by Google on its Search Central website today, Google will provide advance notice of significant search engine ranking updates and actionable policy changes via the Search Status Dashboard.
  • It has been revealed that according to the main page of the fresh Ranking Hub section of Search Central, the purpose of these announcements is to give site owners “predictability and time to prepare” when it comes to how and when their rankings may be affected by a Google revision.
  • I wrote about both the CMA’s requirement this past June and, this morning, Google’s announcement of an upcoming revision to their algorithms, the December 2026 core update.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that according to a latest ranking section released by Google on its Search Central website today, Google will provide advance notice of significant search engine ranking updates and actionable policy changes via the Search Status Dashboard. In addition, for each ranking update announced on the Search Status Dashboard, you can now provide Google with your thoughts through Search Console.

It has been revealed that according to the main page of the fresh Ranking Hub section of Search Central, the purpose of these announcements is to give site owners “predictability and time to prepare” when it comes to how and when their rankings may be affected by a Google revision. If a particular ranking update has the potential to cause major changes in search engine rankings within the United Kingdom, then advance notice regarding those types of updates follows UK governmental requirements placed upon Google in June (via the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority, or CMA) requiring fair ranking practices, according to a second page.

I wrote about both the CMA’s requirement this past June and, this morning, Google’s announcement of an upcoming revision to their algorithms, the December 2026 core update.

Two types of changes that get notice are listed by Google in its page on staying informed about ranking updates. The first is actionable policy updates, which include updates to content policies, technical guidelines or eligibility rules that could result in site owners having to make edits to their pages, content practices or markup. The second is significant ranking changes, broad updates like core updates that may move rankings across many queries and sites.

“Additionally, for changes where UK people may experience a significant ranking shift, we provide advance notice to site owners in accordance with CMA’s fair ranking conduct requirements for Google.”.

Google says you can find pre-announcements, rollout start dates, and completion notices on the Search Status Dashboard, which also offers an RSS feed.

Recent findings suggest that the Dashboard’s Nov. 24 entry preannounced the December 2026 core update and listed December as the release window.

The CMA’s rules set minimum notice periods for changes that reach UK consumers.

In a recent development, according to the CMA’s summary of the requirement, Google must give at least 30 business days’ notice before changes where publishers could act to avoid or reduce the impact on their ranking. Other changes that may move rankings significantly, where Google can explain what is changing and why, need at least 15 business days. The requirement comes into force Dec. 17, so these minimums aren’t binding yet.

Google’s stay-informed page claims it explains “our advance notice timelines,” but it doesn’t list how many days.

In a recent development, according to Google’s feedback page, if you are a verified owner of your website, then you may submit feedback about a significant ranking change or a new actionable policy revision listed in the Search Status Dashboard. Your feedback would go through the Submit Feedback button in Search Console, with the name of the change referenced in the #hashtag format, such as #NovemberCoreUpdate2026.

It has been revealed that on this same page, Google suggests listing a snapshot of the Performance report, the search queries and URLs impacted by the change, and the URLs of sites that seem to be ranking for those searches in error. Google also suggests noting how the change affected “the functioning of a UK market in which you are active.”.

Google states its engineering teams evaluate submissions as a whole and do not make manual URL-specific ranking changes based upon such feedback.

Lastly, this webpage includes information regarding a UK CMA indexing appeal. As of Dec. 17, sites serving UK consumers that have been manually removed from Google’s index entirely will be allowed to file appeals. Under requirements set forth by the CMA, Google must provide these websites with another option to resolve their disputes.

Sources indicate that google’s principles page says AI Overviews and other result types are judged by the same criteria as web listings. Google wrote:.

“This means that web page listings and other results like AI Overviews, carousels, images, and videos are evaluated using the same criteria. No result receives preferential treatment.”.

The page also notes Google doesn’t make manual ranking adjustments except to comply with legal obligations or apply its Content Policies for Search.

When you add the Search Status Dashboard’s RSS feed to your monitoring, you will receive notification of a preannounced ranking update before your rankings change.

The stay-informed page on Google notes to allow at least one week of post-rollout data, after an update is marked complete, prior to analyzing changes in traffic. The first full week after November’s core update would be from Nov. 25 through Dec. 1. Feedback submitted by you, which includes the recommended Performance report data as well as the queries, URLs and the #NovemberCoreUpdate2026 tag, can be submitted after this date.

Dec. 17 is when the CMA requirement comes into force and the UK appeal link goes live. The December core upgrade’s start date will go on the dashboard when the rollout begins.

Google also published two generative AI pages today, one on the controls for how content is used in its AI features and one on how AI Overviews and AI Mode select and link sources.

According to recent reports, liveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

Industry observers note that our customers trust us with audio, video and data belonging to their own end owners, so a security failure on our side puts their data and their business at risk. We are hiring a Security Engineer to build and run our vulnerability management and security operations program. Vulnerability management is a core capability for keeping our security posture strong as the platform and the firm grow: knowing what we run, finding what is exposed, and getting the right fixes shipped promptly. It also underpins our customer commitments and the compliance programs we are building. Our program is early, and you will shape it. You will join a small Trust team that covers security, IT and compliance, and you will own this program end to end from your first week.

think like both a builder and a breaker, and understand security from first principles.

take an automation-first and pragmatic approach to risk mitigation.

translate security concerns into engineering action.

can clearly explain complex technical concepts to others.

are a fast learner and thrive in ambiguity.

Select, deploy and operationalize scanning tooling across our production assets.

Run vulnerability management end to end: triage, severity in our environment, owner assignment, remediation SLAs and reporting.

Build engineering-first triage and remediation workflows that fit how our engineering teams already work, and automate the routing and follow-up.

Build a remediation dashboard that engineering and leadership read and act on.

Automate collection of the vulnerability management evidence our compliance programs depend on, in partnership with our Compliance team.

Build automation, including agentic tooling, that removes manual security operations work and keeps pace with engineering growth.

5+ years in security engineering, security operations or software engineering, with a significant share of that focused on security.

Hands-on experience building or running a vulnerability management program or software security tooling (SCA, container, cloud or host scanning).

An engineering-first approach to triage and remediation: you get findings fixed by making the fix easy to ship.

The judgment to set a finding's real severity in our environment, using CVSS as one input.

Strong scripting and automation skills in a language such as Go or Python, and comfort reading infrastructure as code such as Terraform.

A pragmatic approach to risk: you can explain why a finding matters to the business and how fast it needs to be fixed.

Experience with real-time media, networking or WebRTC systems.

Experience supporting compliance audits such as HIPAA, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001 or SOC 2.

Incident response or application security experience.

Experience in AI security, such as securing LLM applications or agent infrastructure.

An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

Industry observers note that the fresh budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”.

A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

That changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

Expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”.

I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

Sources indicate that “We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan stated. “They see what Major Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”.

Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s big local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a fresh tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

The labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

“In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

“That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan remarked. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”.

In the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

But News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

The Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Debuted in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

Even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results showed the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

“Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

In a recent development, many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”.

“Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he said.

Some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

It has been revealed that deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

“To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan said.

The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

It has been revealed that “When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan mentioned. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”.

#159702. AI Visibility Is Not A Recommendation – GEO Needs To Measure Decisions via @sejournal, @billhunt

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3208 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

AI Visibility Is Not A Recommendation – GEO Needs To Measure Decisions via @sejournal, @billhunt

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, recent research is raising questions about the commercial value of AI visibility.
  • It has been revealed that rand Fishkin recently asked whether AI visibility is becoming a marketing boondoggle.
  • It has been revealed that I understand the skepticism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, recent research is raising questions about the commercial value of AI visibility. It also exposes a problem with what we have chosen to measure.

It has been revealed that rand Fishkin recently asked whether AI visibility is becoming a marketing boondoggle. In a Whiteboard video shared on LinkedIn, he discussed several studies questioning the commercial returns from visibility in standalone AI assistants, while distinguishing those platforms from Google’s AI-powered search experiences.

It has been revealed that I understand the skepticism. We have seen an extraordinary amount of enthusiasm for GEO measurement, accompanied by upcoming tools, new metrics, and a growing expectation that brands should monitor how often they appear in AI-generated answers. Much of that work is useful. I want to know whether a firm appears when prospective customers search for its category, how its capabilities are presented, and which competitors are recommended.

In a recent development, for some time, I have been concerned that we are investing heavily in tracking mentions, citations, and share of voice without giving enough attention to the decisions customers are asking AI systems to help them make. We seem to have accepted that being mentioned is inherently valuable, even when we cannot demonstrate that the mention helped a customer evaluate the tech giant or move toward a purchase.

Recent findings suggest that I’m also concerned about this given the executive attention SEO, GEO, and AEO are receiving. Search professionals have spent years trying to secure the resources and cross-functional cooperation needed to make meaningful changes. Now, in some organizations, we have senior leadership listening, budgets for tools and content, and an unusual willingness to bring marketing, product, sales, and technical teams together.

According to recent reports, we risk squandering that opportunity if the principal outcome we report is more AI visibility. Executives are investing because they believe AI is changing how customers discover and choose vendors. We need to show that our work is addressing that change, not simply producing another set of exposure metrics.

The starting point is the customer’s motivation. People generally aren’t going to ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google’s AI-powered search experiences for another page of links. They want help understanding something, comparing alternatives, or reaching a decision. Traditional search left much of that work to the user, who had to visit multiple sites and reconcile the information. AI systems are attractive partly because they reduce that effort.

Recent findings suggest that yet we still talk about GEO as though the expected journey is a brand mention, followed by a click, followed by a conversion. That sequence may describe some purchases, but it is a poor model for many complex B2B decisions.

It has been revealed that fishkin’s argument drew on research from Marie Haynes, The SEO Works, and Kevin Indig. Although they approached the problem differently, their findings make it difficult to assume that increasing visibility in standalone AI assistants will necessarily produce meaningful traffic or conversions.

According to recent reports, in GEO Is a Distraction, Haynes examined analytics data from 100 websites representing more than 145 million sessions. ChatGPT referrals accounted for approximately 0.62% of Google organic sessions, rising to 0.73% when other tracked language models were included. Even when ChatGPT visitors converted at higher rates, the difference in traffic volume meant that Google organic traffic remained far more key to measured conversions.

Her concern is partly one of priorities. Given the changes taking place within Google Search, how much effort should businesses devote to improving visibility in standalone assistants that right now contribute relatively little measurable traffic?

It has been revealed that the SEO Works’ AI Referral Traffic Benchmark examined 95 websites and found that organic search generated 39 times as many sessions as AI assistants. For every 100 conversions attributed to organic search, AI referrals generated 3.2. The study also found considerable variation in conversion performance. Although AI referrals converted approximately 18% better overall, the rate for B2B product companies was only 0.62 times that of organic traffic.

That last finding caught my attention because B2B buying behavior is often discussed as though AI-assisted discovery will naturally produce exceptionally valuable visits. I agree it may, but only if the information is available, and I note that it might not be universally applicable.

Kevin Indig explored another possibility in Does AI Drive More Direct Traffic?. Perhaps AI influences buyers who subsequently visit a website directly or search for a brand, leaving the original influence unattributed. In an analysis of 12 analytics properties, he found that some apparent direct-traffic growth was due to bot activity. Additional testing across four brands and 632 tests did not establish a reliable relationship between AI visibility and subsequent direct or branded search activity.

Indig did not argue that AI has no influence on purchasing behavior. Rather, his work demonstrated how difficult it is to establish that influence using the signals available in conventional analytics.

Sources indicate that I think these findings deserve more than a debate about whether GEO is worth the investment. They should prompt us to reconsider what we are asking visibility metrics to prove.

If a customer uses AI to compare vendors, rule out unsuitable products, or validate a shortlist, there may be no referral click. The customer could make substantial progress toward a decision without visiting any of the cited sources. That does not mean the AI interaction had no value, but it also does not mean every brand mentioned in the response benefited commercially.

The question I want to answer is what happened during the evaluation, particularly whether the firm had enough supporting evidence to be considered a suitable choice.

See also: AI Visibility Measurement: What To Track & What To Ignore.

A recent conversation with an executive brought this into focus for me. He was evaluating outside consulting support and explained that his organization had been disappointed by consultants and vendors three times in the previous year. He was not interested in another polished sales pitch or a broad claim of expertise. Having been burned repeatedly, he intended to make the next selection process considerably more demanding.

According to recent reports, what stood out was his sense of responsibility for the decision. He needed to be confident that the next consultant could deliver, but he also needed to justify that confidence to the organization.

We sometimes underestimate how much of a complex purchasing decision is about avoiding risk. Buyers are trying to establish that a product will work in their environment, meet the requirements of different stakeholders, and avoid creating problems they will later have to explain. When budgets are tight, the consequences of getting that decision wrong become even more significant.

A company can be well-known, highly visible, and frequently mentioned without addressing those concerns.

Consider a buyer evaluating specialized software. Knowing that a vendor is a recognized provider may be useful at the beginning of the process. Once the buyer introduces requirements involving integrations, compliance, implementation capacity, or operational constraints, general category visibility becomes much less informative. The buyer needs evidence that the vendor can satisfy those requirements.

This is where I believe the distinction between appearing in an answer and earning a recommendation becomes commercially important.

See also: 3 Steps To Win B2B Brand Consideration, Day Zero Decides The Shortlist.

Sources indicate that we saw this problem in an engagement with a specialized B2B software company. Across the AI responses we observed, the brand was cited 98% of the time. By most visibility measures, that would be considered an excellent result. The company was clearly being recognized within its category.

At the same time, it was receiving little observable AI referral traffic, and its lead volume was declining. We could not establish that AI had caused the decline, but the situation prompted us to look more closely at what happened when buyers moved beyond broad-category questions.

We began testing more specific decision scenarios, introducing the requirements that a prospective customer might use to determine which vendors to include on a shortlist. Under those conditions, the company’s recommendation rate was 17%. In a separate testing condition where supporting evidence was absent, the rate was 8%.

As we examined the responses, we found that vital capabilities were not always supported by information the AI systems could retrieve. In a workshop reviewing those gaps, someone on the client team noted, “We have all of that. We just don’t have it on the website.”.

I have heard variations of that statement throughout my career, but it takes on a different significance when customers can use AI to evaluate vendors before speaking with sales.

There are often legitimate reasons information is not publicly available. Some details are commercially sensitive. Some capabilities are complex enough that sales or technical teams prefer to explain them directly. Other information simply never makes it onto the website because nobody has recognized its importance to the buying decision.

It has been revealed that historically, a website could generate interest and leave the lead nurturing to sales. As research has shown, especially in B2B, AI-assisted evaluation often takes place before the buyer makes contact, creating a significant disadvantage. The firm may satisfy the requirement, yet the available evidence may not be sufficient to establish that suitability.

The answer is not to just publish everything but to clearly identify the requirements customers are likely to evaluate and determine what credible, appropriately disclosed evidence can support those assessments.

See also: B2B Buyers Choose A Vendor Before They Reach Out – 3 Ways To Be Visible When It Counts.

This is the thinking behind the Decision Coverage framework I introduced in Decision Coverage: Why AI Recommends Some Brands And Not Others.

In an earlier article, When AI Takes The Click, Click Worthiness Should Guide Your Strategy, I argued that marketers should focus more attention on interactions where direct engagement still adds meaningful value after AI has answered an informational question. Decision Coverage approaches the problem from the other side: before a customer engages directly, have we made enough evidence available for our firm to be evaluated accurately?

Industry observers note that one useful concept is the eligibility gate, a requirement that a solution must meet to be considered suitable for a particular buyer. This is a way to model purchasing decisions, not a claim that language models use a fixed internal checklist.

In a recent development, A buyer might regard some capabilities as desirable and others as mandatory. If a vendor cannot satisfy a critical requirement, it may not belong on the shortlist, regardless of how visible it is. But there is another possibility that marketers need to recognize: the vendor meets the requirement, yet the supporting evidence is missing or difficult to retrieve.

Recent findings suggest that traditional content-gap analysis does not always uncover this problem. We may find that a competitor has written about a topic we have not covered, or that our pages need stronger explanations of a product category. Those findings can improve discoverability, but they may have little bearing on whether a buyer can establish that we meet a mandatory requirement.

Decision Coverage starts with the decision itself. What is the customer trying to accomplish? Who is involved? Which requirements are essential, which are negotiable, and what trade-offs are likely to influence the choice? We can then examine whether the information available about the company is sufficient to support an assessment against those criteria.

This requires significantly more cooperation across the business than many traditional SEO activities. Marketing may understand the buyer persona, but product teams often hold the evidence needed to answer them, and most importantly, sales understands the prospects’ objections and evaluation criteria.

Sources indicate that that is another reason I am concerned about wasting the current level of executive attention. We finally have an opportunity to bring these groups together around a problem that matters to customers. I would rather use that access to close important evidence gaps than simply produce more category content.

Sources indicate that our research into AI fan-out questions gave us another reason to focus on decision criteria. In one study beginning with a prompt asking for the best solution in a software category, 62% of the observed questions concerned understanding the category, developing evaluation criteria, or comparing vendors.

According to recent reports, those observations do not reveal a model’s complete internal reasoning, and I would not suggest that every AI system follows the same process. What they show is that the observable research supporting a recommendation can involve considerably more than retrieving a list of vendors.

Industry observers note that we also found that recommendations sometimes changed when we altered the buyer’s perspective. A prompt framed around an individual’s professional responsibilities did not always produce the same recommendations as one written from the perspective of a department or organization.

Sources indicate that in another test, a vendor appeared as the leading recommendation until we changed the emphasis and ordering of the requirements. That vendor then disappeared from the recommended set, replaced by a tech giant that had not previously appeared but was particularly strong on the newly emphasized criterion.

Industry observers note that I cannot attribute that change solely to the order of the requirements, as we saw other cases where retests days later prompted different interpretations, putting focus on different criteria. Nevertheless, the results made it difficult to defend the idea that recommendation performance could be represented adequately by a single broad prompt or a static collection of category queries.

That is why understanding decision context matters. A tech giant may be the strongest option for one combination of requirements and less suitable when another constraint takes priority. Unfortunately, we don’t have unlimited budgets for every conceivable prompt, but we can maybe use larger diagnostic prompts that capture multiple prompt turns.

According to recent reports, accordingly, for measurement and alignment purposes, I would rather test a representative set of buyer decisions than simply increase the number of prompts being tracked. The objective is to understand when the firm qualifies, where evidence is missing, and which competing vendors are better supported for particular requirements. Those are the critical insights we need to understand to truly close gaps.

Sources indicate that mike King also raises a related measurement glitch in How Do We Move Forward if the SERP Is Generative?. As search results become dynamically generated, he argues that conventional assumptions about stable rankings are increasingly difficult to maintain. Measuring visibility requires repeated observations and a probabilistic approach rather than relying on a single result.

I agree, and I think recommendation measurement needs to account for another source of variation: the customer’s requirements.

Recent findings suggest that A firm might appear in nearly every broad category response but be recommended infrequently for the decision scenarios that matter most to its business. Another company might have lower overall visibility but be consistently recommended when its particular strengths align with the buyer’s needs. Aggregated mention counts cannot adequately explain either situation.

It has been revealed that for our B2B software client, the evidence gaps suggested a testable hypothesis. If the firm genuinely satisfies crucial buyer requirements but has not made that information retrievable, improving the available evidence should increase its recommendation frequency under comparable decision scenarios.

Recent findings suggest that we can establish a baseline, address specific gaps, and repeat the testing. Because generated responses vary, that work needs multiple observations and consistent scenarios rather than a few favorable examples.

I want to be careful about what an improvement would mean, however. A higher recommendation rate would suggest that the available evidence is better supporting the organization’s suitability. It would not prove that buyers are choosing the company more often or that the work has increased revenue.

That distinction matters especially for this client, whose sales cycle typically lasts 9 to 14 months. Even if better evidence starts influencing evaluations now, we may not see the corresponding effect on qualified opportunities or pipeline for several quarters. Some buyers may already have made their decisions while important information was missing.

We also have to recognize that the decline in leads could have several causes. Market demand, product competitiveness, sales execution, and other marketing activity may all be influencing performance. The combination of declining leads and weak recommendation performance is a reason to investigate, not evidence of causation.

Sources indicate that I would therefore measure progress in stages. First, determine whether the gaps in decision-support evidence have actually been closed. Then test whether recommendation performance changes in the scenarios where those gaps mattered. Over time, examine whether qualified opportunities, pipeline, and eventually revenue show corresponding improvements, while considering other factors that could explain the results.

It has been revealed that customer interviews and self-reported discovery information may help fill some of the attribution gaps. They will not provide perfect answers, but they can help us understand whether AI-assisted research played a role in the buying process. This is consistent with Indig’s broader finding that neither referral traffic nor changes in direct traffic can explain AI’s commercial influence on their own.

Industry observers note that I would not make AI referral traffic the primary KPI for this work. If the customer can reach an evaluation or shortlist decision without clicking, referral counts may tell us relatively little about whether our information helped or hindered that decision.

According to recent reports, I think Fishkin is right to challenge the industry on business value. The findings from Haynes, The SEO Works, and Indig should make marketers cautious about presenting increased AI visibility as evidence of commercial success. King’s work also reminds us that the visibility we are trying to measure is becoming less stable and more dependent on context.

My concern is that we will respond by building increasingly sophisticated visibility dashboards without addressing what happens when a buyer asks whether a company is actually suitable.

Recent findings suggest that for complex purchases, that question is often more crucial than whether the brand appeared in an earlier answer. Customers are trying to reduce risk, compare alternatives, and make defensible decisions. If AI systems are helping them do that work, our responsibility is to make sure the information available about our companies supports an accurate evaluation.

It has been revealed that this is also an opportunity for search professionals to expand their contribution. The attention GEO is receiving has created access to people and resources that were often difficult to engage through conventional SEO initiatives. We can use that access to work with product, sales, technical, and legal teams to identify what customers need to establish and make appropriate evidence available.

I do need to know whether a brand is being discovered and represented accurately, but more importantly, I want to know whether the brand is recommended when it genuinely meets a buyer’s requirements, what evidence supports that recommendation, and where missing information may be limiting consideration.

If we can improve those leading indicators and then establish, over time, that they contribute to higher-quality opportunities and better commercial outcomes, we will have a much stronger argument for GEO investment than mention counts alone can provide.

The question is not whether AI visibility has value. It is whether we are confusing being present in an answer with being considered in a decision.
